title: Array Prototype Last
statement:
Give every array a method `last()`: calling `nums.last()` on any array returns its final element, or `-1` when the array has no elements. The method must work on arrays that already exist as well as on every array created later, so it belongs on `Array.prototype`. Return the element as it is, whatever it holds (a number, a string, `null`, an object, another array), and leave the array unchanged.

Each case gives one array `nums`, built by `JSON.parse`, and the answer is what `nums.last()` returns.
constraints: nums is a valid JSON array
notes:
## Intuition

Every array inherits from `Array.prototype`. When code calls `nums.last()`, JavaScript looks for `last` on `nums` itself, does not find it, and then looks on `Array.prototype`. So one function stored there becomes a method of every array, including arrays created before the assignment, because the lookup happens at call time. Inside a method called as `nums.last()`, `this` is `nums`. The last element sits at index `length - 1`, and an empty array has none. (The brute force walks the whole array instead, remembering the latest element it sees.)

## Approach

1. Assign a regular `function` (not an arrow function) to `Array.prototype.last`, so that `this` is the array it is called on.
2. If `this.length` is `0`, return `-1`.
3. Otherwise return `this[this.length - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums` is `[null, {}, 3]`.

- `nums.last` is not an own property of `nums`, so the lookup finds it on `Array.prototype`, and the call runs with `this` set to `nums`.
- `this.length` is `3`, not `0`, so the empty case is skipped.
- `this[3 - 1]` is `3`, which is returned.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1): one length check and one index.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- With an arrow function, `this` is not the array, because arrow functions take `this` from the surrounding code.
- `return this[this.length - 1] || -1` turns a final `0`, `""` or `false` into `-1`, and `?? -1` does the same to a final `null`. Decide by the length, not by the element.
- `this.pop()` returns the right value but removes it from the array.
- Plain assignment makes `last` an enumerable property, so a `for...in` loop over any array lists it. `Object.defineProperty(Array.prototype, 'last', { value: ..., writable: true, configurable: true })` avoids that. In shared code, extending built-in prototypes also risks clashing with future standard methods.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `this` | the array that `last()` was called on |
| `this.length` | how many elements it has; the last one is at index `length - 1` |

narration.1: Store a regular function on Array.prototype, so every array, old or new, finds last through its prototype.
narration.2: this is the array last was called on; an empty array has no last element.
narration.3: Return -1, the agreed answer for an empty array.
narration.5: Otherwise the last element sits at index length - 1; return it as it is, even if it is null, 0 or an object.
narration.6: The assignment ends here; from now on every array has a last method.
